items.q: In the expand → migrate → verify → contract pattern, what does the EXPAND phase ship?

options.t: The new store plus dual writes, while reads stay on the old store
options.why: Right. Expand adds the new destination alongside the old and starts writing both. Nothing user-visible changes — reads still come from the old store, which stays the source of truth.

options.t: The backfill job that copies all historical rows into the new store in resumable batches
options.why: That's MIGRATE. Backfill only makes sense after dual writes are on — otherwise rows changed during the copy would be missed.

options.t: The feature flag that flips reads to the new store
options.why: That's CONTRACT, the last phase. Flipping reads before the new store is populated and verified would serve users empty or wrong data.

options.t: A maintenance window announcement
options.why: The whole pattern exists to avoid the window. Global traffic and SLO error budgets killed the 'down for maintenance Sunday' approach.

items.q: Your SLO is 99.95% monthly. Roughly how much downtime does that allow, and what does it say about a 4-hour maintenance window?

options.t: About 22 minutes — the window spends roughly a year of error budget
options.why: Correct. 0.05% of a month is ~22 minutes. A 240-minute planned outage is about 11 months of budget on one change — which is why SLO-run shops migrate live instead.

options.t: About 4 hours — the window exactly fits
options.why: That would be roughly a 99.4% SLO. At 99.95% you get minutes per month, not hours — the arithmetic is the argument against windows.

options.t: About 22 minutes, but planned downtime doesn't count against SLOs
options.why: Comforting and wrong as a default. Users experience planned downtime identically to an outage, and most SLO definitions count it. Exemptions exist but must be negotiated, not assumed.

options.t: SLOs only apply to unplanned incidents
options.why: An SLO is a promise about user experience, not about your intentions. A user who can't check out doesn't care whether the outage was scheduled.

items.q: During the migration, which store is the source of truth, and until when?

options.t: The new store, as soon as dual writes begin
options.why: Backwards — at that point the new store is an unverified shadow with no history. Treating it as truth means serving users from an incomplete copy.

options.t: The old store, until the cutover in the contract phase
options.why: Yes. All reads come from the old store through expand, migrate, and verify. The new store is a shadow being warmed up — it can be wrong for a while and no user ever sees it.

options.t: Both equally — that's what dual write means
options.why: Dual WRITE, single TRUTH. Two equal sources of truth is precisely the failure state this chapter warns about; one store must be authoritative at every instant.

options.t: Whichever store acknowledged the most recent write first, since it holds the freshest data
options.why: That would make truth nondeterministic per request. The authority is a design decision made once and stated out loud, not a race.

items.q: Select every property a production backfill job must have. (Choose all that apply.)

options.t: Rate-limited, throttling on signals like replica lag
options.why: Yes — a backfill that outruns replication takes the read path down as collateral damage. gh-ost made lag-based throttling a headline feature for exactly this reason.

options.t: Resumable from a durable checkpoint
options.why: Yes — a multi-day job WILL die mid-run (deploy, OOM, reclaimed instance). 'Done through key X' recorded after each batch turns a disaster into a shrug.

options.t: Idempotent, with writes conditional on version so newer data survives
options.why: Yes — batches get retried and race live dual writes. A blind upsert can overwrite tonight's data with last year's; comparing a version or updated_at prevents it.

options.t: Wrapped in a single transaction covering the whole table
options.why: A transaction spanning billions of rows would hold locks for days and could never commit. Small independent batches are the entire point — the job is safe because each piece is tiny and repeatable.

items.q: What is a shadow read?

options.t: A read served from a replica instead of the primary
options.why: That's just a replica read (Chapter 1.8). Shadow reads are about comparing two stores during a migration, not about which node serves.

options.t: A cached read that may be stale
options.why: Staleness is a caching concern. A shadow read is a verification technique — the second read exists only to be compared, never to be served.

options.t: Reading both stores, serving the old answer, and counting disagreements
options.why: Exactly. The user always gets the old store's answer, so nothing can regress; the comparison happens in the background and feeds a mismatch metric that gates the cutover.

options.t: A read performed by the backfill job to find rows it has not yet copied into the new store
options.why: The backfill reads by key range to copy data. Shadow reads run on real production requests, which is what makes them representative of what users would actually see.

items.q: Why is a plain ALTER TABLE on a 400M-row MySQL table risky even with modern 'online DDL'?

options.t: Rebuilding a table that large silently corrupts its secondary indexes, forcing a restore from backup
options.why: No — ALTER is correct, just disruptive. The danger is availability (locks, lag), not data corruption.

options.t: It can wedge on a metadata lock, queueing every query behind it, and lags replicas for the duration
options.why: Right. One long-running query can block the ALTER's metadata lock, and everything behind it queues — the app just stops. Meanwhile replicas apply the ALTER serially and fall far behind.

options.t: MySQL forbids ALTER on tables over 100M rows
options.why: There's no such limit. MySQL will happily run it — the pain is operational, which is why tools like gh-ost exist rather than error messages.

options.t: ALTER only works inside a maintenance window
options.why: Nothing enforces a window; the risk is that a naive ALTER quietly CREATES one — a self-scheduled incident. The fix is a ghost-table migration, not a banner.

items.q: What is the key design difference between gh-ost and trigger-based tools like pt-online-schema-change?

options.t: gh-ost tails the binary log instead of putting triggers on the live table
options.why: Yes. Triggers run inside your production write transactions, adding latency and lock contention you can't pause. gh-ost reads the binlog — often from a replica — so the live write path is untouched and the migration can throttle, pause, and resume.

options.t: gh-ost is faster because it skips verification
options.why: Neither faster-by-skipping nor true — gh-ost's advantage is control (throttle, pause, deferred cut-over), not cut corners.

options.t: gh-ost rewrites rows in place, so it never needs to build and swap a full copy of the table
options.why: Both approaches build a ghost/shadow copy with the new schema and swap at the end. The difference is how live changes reach that copy: triggers versus binlog replay.

options.t: pt-online-schema-change only works on PostgreSQL
options.why: Both tools are MySQL-family tools. Postgres has different mechanisms (instant nullable columns, concurrent index builds) and its own tooling.

items.q: Why is the read cutover done with a feature flag rather than a code deploy?

options.t: Flags are easier to code-review than deploys
options.why: Review effort isn't the issue. The operational property that matters is reaction time when something goes wrong mid-cutover.

options.t: A flag flips in seconds without shipping code, and supports percentage rollout
options.why: Right. Rollback becomes a runtime toggle measured in seconds, not a deploy measured in minutes — and you can expose 1% of users first, watch, and ramp. The flag IS the rollback plan.

options.t: Deploys are forbidden during migrations
options.why: Deploys continue normally throughout a migration — each phase ships as one. The flag specifically decouples the risky flip from the deploy machinery.

options.t: Flags avoid having to verify the new store first
options.why: Nothing skips verification — the flag flips only after the mismatch metric has sat at ~zero for days. The flag controls exposure; the metric grants permission.

items.q: When is it safe to actually delete the old store or column?

options.t: Immediately after reads hit 100% on the new store and the first hour of dashboards stays green
options.why: That's the moment your rollback path still matters most — day-three silent corruption is a real pattern. Deleting now welds the exit shut.

options.t: As soon as the backfill completes
options.why: At backfill completion the new store hasn't served a single production read. Verification and gradual cutover both stand between here and deletion.

options.t: Weeks after cutover, once everything has been stable and the old store is snapshotted
options.why: Yes. The old path outlives the flip deliberately: burn-in time catches late-discovered problems, the snapshot is the final parachute, and only then does contract finish.

options.t: Never — keep it forever as a backup
options.why: 'Forever' is the dual-write trap wearing a safety costume: two schemas to maintain, drifting copies, doubled write cost. Contract has a date; backups are snapshots, not live parallel systems.

items.q: During expand, your write to the NEW store fails for one request (old-store write succeeded). What should the code do?

options.t: Fail the user's request so the stores stay consistent
options.why: This couples production availability to an unproven shadow system — the warming-up copy can now take down checkout. The old store is the truth; its success means the request succeeded.

options.t: Retry synchronously until the new store accepts it
options.why: Blocking a live user on an unlimited retry against a non-authoritative store turns a shadow's bad day into user-facing latency. Bound the work, then hand off.

options.t: Succeed the request; log the miss for repair and let verification catch drift
options.why: Right. Old store first and authoritative; new store best-effort with failures recorded. The mismatch metric exists precisely because dual writes leak — the design absorbs it.

options.t: Roll back the old-store write to keep the copies identical
options.why: Undoing a committed, user-visible write to protect a shadow copy inverts the hierarchy of truth — and introduces its own failure window. The copy serves the migration, never the other way around.

items.q: Verifier finds rows where the new store holds OLDER data than the old store. Backfill and dual writes both ran. Most likely cause?

options.t: The backfill's stale copies landed last, blind-upserting over fresher dual-written rows
options.why: The classic race. Read at T0, dual-write at T1, stale write at T2 — no errors anywhere, wrong data everywhere. The fix is conditional writes: apply only if the incoming version is newer than what's stored.

options.t: The new store is dropping writes randomly
options.why: Random drops would show as MISSING rows, not systematically older ones. Older-data-present is the signature of a stale writer winning a race.

options.t: Replica lag on the old store is feeding the verifier stale values, so the comparison itself is wrong
options.why: Lag would make a reader see slightly old data from the OLD store's replicas — it doesn't explain the new store holding superseded values after both pipelines wrote.

options.t: The verifier is comparing in the wrong direction
options.why: Always worth a sanity check, but 'new is older than old' on specific recently-updated rows is too precise a pattern — it points at the backfill/dual-write interleave, the most common real-world bug in this pattern.

items.q: Shadow reads show a steady 0.01% mismatch rate for a week — about 100K disagreements/day at your volume. The team wants to cut over; 99.99% agreement 'seems fine.' Call?

options.t: Cut over — no migration is perfect
options.why: A STEADY rate is never noise; it's a systematic bug (nulls, timezones, encoding) living in a slice of your data. Cutting over ships 100K wrong answers a day and calls it done.

options.t: Hold: sample the mismatches, find the bug class, fix, re-backfill that slice
options.why: Right. Steady-state mismatches cluster by cause — a handful of logged samples usually reveals one bug. The gate is ~zero held for days because that's the only number that means 'the copy is actually equivalent.'

options.t: Cut over but keep shadow reads running to monitor it
options.why: Monitoring a known bug in the serving path isn't mitigation — users now RECEIVE the wrong answers you're gracefully counting. Verification's whole point is catching this while the old store still serves.

options.t: Keep serving from the old store and extend the verification window by another month to be safe
options.why: More watching won't change a steady rate — the bug doesn't fix itself. This hedges instead of diagnosing; the senior move is to go read the mismatch samples today.

items.q: Resharding user_id % 4 → user_id % 16: where can rows from old shard 2 land, and why does it matter?

options.t: Any of the 16 — modulo scatters uniformly
options.why: Uniform overall, but constrained per row: x % 4 = 2 forces x % 16 into {2, 6, 10, 14}. Missing this means planning a 16-way shuffle when a clean 4-way split is available.

options.t: Only new shard 2 — matching remainders stay together
options.why: Only user_ids with x % 16 = 2 stay; the rest of old shard 2 spreads to 6, 10, and 14. If nothing moved, the reshard wouldn't relieve anything.

options.t: New shards {2, 6, 10, 14} — each old shard splits into exactly four children
options.why: Yes: x % 4 = 2 constrains x % 16 to that set. No row crosses between old shards, so backfill runs as four independent streams, verification pairs cleanly, and a bad row implicates exactly one stream. Multiplying the shard count is why the split is clean.

options.t: New shards {0, 4, 8, 12} — offsets shift by the old count
options.why: Those are old shard 0's children. The remainder mod 4 is preserved inside the remainder mod 16, so shard 2's children all keep remainder 2 when reduced mod 4.

items.q: Mid-backfill, replica lag climbs from 2s to 45s and read-path staleness alerts fire. First move?

options.t: Throttle or pause the backfill and let replication drain
options.why: The backfill is the new variable and the only discretionary load — it must yield to production. This is why lag-based throttling is built into serious tools; ideally the job slows itself before humans get paged.

options.t: Add more replicas to absorb the write volume
options.why: Replicas don't absorb writes — each one must apply the same stream, so new replicas start behind and lag too. Capacity is a later conversation; the immediate fix is reducing the discretionary load.

options.t: Push through — the backfill finishes sooner if it keeps its rate
options.why: Finishing 10% sooner while serving stale reads for hours inverts priorities. The system being migrated must stay healthy THROUGH the migration; the calendar is the flexible resource.

options.t: Fail over reads to the primary until the backfill completes
options.why: Piling the replica read load onto the primary that's already hosting the backfill risks converting lag into a full outage. Contain the cause, don't rearrange the victims.

items.q: Why flip READS to the new store before flipping WRITES?

options.t: Reads are more important to users than writes
options.why: Importance isn't the logic — reversibility is. The ordering exists because of what stays true while both stores are written.

options.t: Both stores stay current under dual writes, so the read flag is reversible in both directions
options.why: Exactly. Reads can move 1% → 100% and back with zero data consequences because both copies keep receiving every write. Flip writes first and the old store starts rotting immediately — read rollback then serves stale data.

options.t: Write flips require a maintenance window
options.why: No window needed — the write flip is also flag-driven, ideally with a reverse dual-write keeping the old store current as the escape hatch. The ordering is about keeping doors two-way, not about windows.

options.t: The new store cannot safely accept authoritative writes until weeks of read traffic have proven it
options.why: It's been accepting writes since expand — that's what dual writing is. What changes at the write flip is which store is authoritative, and you only promote a store that's already serving all reads cleanly.

items.q: Eight months after 'finishing' a migration, a team still dual-writes both stores; reads moved long ago. During incidents, the stores disagree. What's the actual state of this system?

options.t: Safely migrated, with a generous backup
options.why: A backup is a snapshot you restore from — not a live, load-bearing, drifting second write path. This 'backup' costs double writes and answers incident questions with contradictions.

options.t: Stuck mid-migration with two sources of truth — the contract phase never ran, and drift is compounding
options.why: Right, and naming it this way is the senior read. Dual-write is a state you pass through, not operate in: every schema change now happens twice, the repair queue went unwatched, and 'which store is right?' has two answers. Contract needed a calendar date before expand shipped.

options.t: Fine — plenty of companies dual-write permanently as a redundancy layer, and incident-time disagreement is normal replication noise
options.why: Real redundancy (replication, Chapter 1.8) has a consistency protocol and one truth. App-level dual writes to divergent schemas have neither — permanence here is entropy with a justification.

options.t: A verification problem — better mismatch metrics would fix it
options.why: Metrics would MEASURE the drift, not resolve it. The defect is organizational: the migration lost its finish line. The fix is completing contract, then deleting the old path.

items.q: For migrating a payments ledger to a new store, why prefer CDC or outbox over app-level dual writes?

options.t: CDC is faster than application writes
options.why: Throughput isn't the argument — CDC adds a relay hop, if anything. The argument is about a gap that no amount of careful app code can fully close.

options.t: It removes the need for a backfill
options.why: CDC captures changes from when you start tailing; history still needs the chunked backfill. The phases don't collapse — only the live-change capture gets more trustworthy.

options.t: The app can crash between its two writes and record nothing; CDC reads the database's own journal, so no committed change can be missed
options.why: Right. Two non-atomic app writes always leave a crash window where the stores silently diverge. CDC (or outbox: event committed in the same transaction) anchors capture to the commit itself — for money, that's the difference between 'unlikely to drift' and 'cannot silently drift.'

options.t: Dual writes are deprecated in modern architectures
options.why: App-level dual writes remain a legitimate, fast-to-ship choice for tolerant data. The senior skill is matching the mechanism to the stakes, not declaring one pattern dead.

items.q: Writes flipped to the new store three days ago. A subtle corruption bug surfaces. Which earlier decision determines whether you can go back without data loss?

options.t: Whether the old store's hardware was kept powered on and its final pre-flip snapshot was retained
options.why: Powered-on but three days stale is a time machine, not a rollback — returning to it discards every write since the flip. Alive isn't the same as current.

options.t: Whether a reverse dual-write kept feeding the old store after the flip
options.why: Yes. New-store-authoritative with the old store still updated best-effort keeps the old copy current, so rollback is a flag flip, not a data reconstruction. 'How do I get back' was decided before the flip — that's the chapter's discipline in one move.

options.t: Whether the backfill job was archived for re-running
options.why: The backfill copies old → new; it can't resurrect three days of writes that only ever landed in the new store. Reverse flow needed a reverse pipe, built in advance.

options.t: Whether the corruption was caught by shadow reads
options.why: Detection matters but was the previous phase's job; this question is about the escape route. A perfectly detected disaster with no path back is still a disaster.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Change the shard key on the live users table, zero downtime — go.' Which opening reads senior?

options.t: "I'd use gh-ost — it's built for online migrations on MySQL."
options.why: Wrong tool, confidently: gh-ost migrates ONE table's schema on one server; resharding moves rows between machines and changes routing. Reaching for a brand name before shaping the problem is the buzzword reflex.

options.t: "There are several viable strategies here — application-level dual writes, CDC-based replication, or a full rebuild from a snapshot with catch-up replay — each with real trade-offs around consistency, operational effort, cutover risk, and rollback story, so I'd want to walk through the options together before committing to one."
options.why: Option-listing without commitment. True, complete, and driverless — the interviewer asked you to GO, and this answer waits for them to pick.

options.t: "Four phases. Expand: new layout live, CDC dual-writes it, old stays truth. Migrate: throttled, checkpointed, idempotent backfill. Verify: shadow reads, cut only at ~zero mismatches. Contract: flag-flip reads in percentages, then writes, delete weeks later. Every phase has a named rollback — want me to zoom into any?"
options.why: Commits to a plan, names all four phases with their disciplines, states the verification gate and per-phase rollback unprompted, and offers depth on demand. This is the calibration list delivered as one confident opening.

options.t: "Honestly, I'd schedule a short window at the lowest-traffic hour — resharding is too risky to do live."
options.why: The premise was zero downtime, and 'too risky to do live' concedes the exact competency being tested. The live pattern IS the risk-management answer: small reversible steps instead of one giant bet.

items.q: The launch depends on your migration, and the PM asks you to skip the verification phase to save two weeks: 'the backfill ran clean, counts match.' Senior response?

options.t: Agree — matching counts are strong evidence, and deadlines are real
options.why: Counts confirm cardinality, not content — a million rows with a broken timezone conversion count perfectly. Cutting over unverified converts unknown bugs into served answers, silently.

options.t: Refuse and escalate — verification is non-negotiable engineering hygiene
options.why: Right instinct, junior delivery. A flat refusal on hygiene grounds invites an authority contest; the senior version prices the risk and redesigns the schedule so the conflict dissolves.

options.t: Compromise: skip shadow reads but spot-check a thousand random rows manually
options.why: A thousand hand-checked rows can't see a 0.1% systematic bug (that's ~1 expected hit), and manual checks don't run on real read traffic — the thing shadow reads uniquely cover. This trades away the instrument that works for one that feels diligent.

options.t: Reframe: "Verification runs in parallel with life, not instead of it — flip 1% behind the flag while shadow reads accumulate, and ramp on the metric. Skipping it doesn't save two weeks; it moves discovery from a dashboard to production incidents."
options.why: Names the real cost of skipping (bugs found by users instead of counters), then restructures so safety and schedule stop competing — percentage rollout means verification and launch overlap. Turning a refusal into a better plan is the senior move.

items.q: An internal admin tool's table — 40K rows, 12 daytime users, no SLO — needs restructuring. A teammate proposes full expand/migrate/contract with CDC and shadow reads. Your call?

options.t: Support it — the four phases are the professional standard for migrations
options.why: The pattern is the standard for systems that can't stop. Applying weeks of ceremony to 40K rows and 12 tolerant users is cargo-culting — process copied without the conditions that justify it.

options.t: Transaction, deploy, announce a 5-minute pause if needed — done this afternoon
options.why: Right. 40K rows migrates in seconds; the blast radius is a dozen colleagues who can wait. Senior judgment scales ceremony DOWN as fluently as up — knowing when the heavyweight pattern is unjustified is the same skill as knowing when it's mandatory.

options.t: Do the four phases anyway as practice for the real thing
options.why: Practicing on company time by quintupling a task's cost isn't judgment, and rehearsal value is low when nothing pushes back — no lag to throttle against, no mismatches to chase. Practice on a staging copy of the big table instead.

options.t: Ask the team to vote on the approach
options.why: The numbers already voted: 40K rows, no SLO, tolerant users. Delegating a decision the data has made reads as discomfort with owning small calls — which predicts discomfort with big ones.

items.q: Read cutover at 50%. p99 is fine, but mismatch alerts fire — confined to rows updated in the last few minutes. First action, and likely cause?

options.t: Flip the read flag back to old, then investigate — likely lag in the pipeline feeding the new store
options.why: Right on both. Recently-updated-rows-only is the signature of capture lag: the CDC/dual-write pipe is behind, so new-store reads serve slightly stale data. The flag exists for this exact moment — take the free rollback first, diagnose without users in the blast zone.

options.t: Push to 100% — partial cutovers cause transient inconsistencies that settle
options.why: Percentage cutover doesn't create mismatches; it REVEALS them on a small audience, which is its job. Ramping into an active alert converts a contained signal into a full-population incident on a hunch.

options.t: Investigate thoroughly first — flapping the flag might mask the evidence
options.why: The mismatch logs, metrics, and pipeline offsets all persist after the flip back; the evidence doesn't evaporate. Debugging while users receive stale answers spends real harm to preserve convenience.

options.t: Restart the backfill to repair the affected rows
options.why: The backfill's job (history) is done — these rows are being updated NOW, and the live pipe is behind. Re-running a bulk copier into an active lag condition adds load and its own race risks; fix the pipe, not the history.

items.q: Your hottest shard hits 90% disk with unexplained growth accelerating; the 4→16 reshard was planned for next quarter. What does the Foursquare 2010 incident teach about sequencing the next two weeks?

options.t: Start the full reshard immediately — it's the root-cause fix
options.why: A multi-week migration racing a disk that fills in days is exactly the Foursquare shape: the fix arrives mid-collapse and executes under emergency conditions, where their chunk moves couldn't even free memory due to fragmentation. Root cause, wrong tempo.

options.t: Buy headroom first — bigger volume, archive cold data, shed load — then run the reshard as the planned project it was
options.why: Right. Cheap reversible moves reset the clock so the migration runs with rehearsals and rollbacks intact. Foursquare's lesson is precisely this: the same operation is routine as a project and catastrophic as a rescue — eleven hours down proved it.

options.t: It teaches nothing current — that was MongoDB in 2010
options.why: The tooling aged; the dynamics didn't. Skewed growth, a resource ceiling, and a live rebalance attempted past the safety margin is a timeless failure shape — Shopify built dedicated tooling (Ghostferry) to keep this exact operation boring.

options.t: Freeze all writes to the hot shard until the reshard completes
options.why: A write freeze on a hot shard IS an outage for those users — self-inflicted, for weeks. You'd be spending certain downtime to avoid possible downtime, which inverts the entire premise of live migration.

items.q: Shadow reads: zero mismatches for a week. Reads and writes flipped, all green. Before dropping the old table, what should still worry you?

options.t: Nothing — the metrics have covered every angle
options.why: The metrics covered every reader that goes through the app's read path. The dangerous readers are the ones that never did.

options.t: Readers that never went through the app: cron jobs, analytics pipelines, other services querying the table directly
options.why: The classic last-step casualty. Shadow reads instrument YOUR code path; the nightly report, the ETL job, and that other team's direct SQL never appeared in any mismatch metric. Audit grants and query logs, migrate the stragglers, snapshot — then drop.

options.t: That the verification week was too short
options.why: More of the same verification finds more of the same nothing — it watches the instrumented path, which is clean. The gap is coverage, not duration; unwatched paths don't improve with waiting.

options.t: Disk space freed by the drop may fragment
options.why: Reclaiming space is a routine operation and roughly the least risky part of the endgame. The irreversible risk is severing a reader nobody instrumented — you learn about it from their outage.

items.q: Two candidates finish the reshard question. A: crisp four-phase walkthrough, rollback named per phase, backfill duration computed, dual-write trap flagged with a contract date. B: everything A said, plus gh-ost cut-over locking internals and a proposal to build a company-wide migration platform with pluggable verifiers — but ran out of time before naming any rollback. Who scores higher for SENIOR, and why?

options.t: B — more depth and platform thinking signal a higher ceiling
options.why: B skipped the load-bearing senior material (reversibility — the 'how do I get back' at every phase) to perform staff-level garnish. Depth stacked on a missing foundation grades as miscalibration, not ceiling.

options.t: A — complete execution of the senior list beats garnish missing its foundation
options.why: Right. The senior bar is executing ONE migration safely: phases, numbers, verification gate, rollback per step, the trap named. A delivered all of it. B's platform talk is real staff material — but only on top of A's list, never instead of it.

options.t: Equal — both clearly know the pattern deeply
options.why: Interviews grade the judgment displayed, not knowledge inferred. An answer with no rollback story fails the rubric's center regardless of what the candidate probably knows — unsaid safety doesn't score.

options.t: B, if the platform design was technically sound
options.why: Soundness can't repair sequencing. Proposing machinery for fifty teams while your one migration has no escape hatch is the exact backwards calibration the chapter warns about — interviewers read it as reciting ambition over practicing safety.
